newsitem.title: UK: UK expects to get what it wants at EU summit-Cook.
newsitem.headline: UK expects to get what it wants at EU summit-Cook.

text.p: Britain is poised to secure a good deal at next week's Amsterdam summit to conclude a new European Union treaty thanks to the constructive stance taken by the new Labour government, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday.

He told parliament that the government had already re-established Britain as a leading player in Europe because, unlike former prime minister John Major's Conservative administration, it was no longer heckling from the sidelines.

"Precisely because this government is not shouting No' to everything out of prejudice, we are listened to with respect when we do say No' to issues that threaten Britain's national interests," Cook said.
He said there would be a lot of hard bargaining before a deal could be clinched to rewrite the EU's rules and revamp its institutions as a prelude to welcoming former communist countries to the bloc.
But he was confident of reaching agreement on four issues of importance for Britain:
-- securing a legal basis, which could not be challenged in the European Court of Justice, for Britain to keep control of its external borders.
-- tougher provisions against fraud in EU member states.
-- a reweighting of votes in the council of ministers to give a louder voice to the bloc's four big countries, including Britain.
-- retaining the national veto in foreign and security policy.
"We can return from Amsterdam not just having done a good deal for Britain but having obtained a better deal for Britain that the previous government could have hoped to achieve," Cook said.

Cook, setting the stage for Prime Minister Tony Blair to declare another victory at Amsterdam, said EU governments had already agreed to put the need for job flexibility and skills at the core of a proposed chapter in the treaty on employment.
Blair has put the drive for flexible labour markets at the core of his government's European policy since he was elected in a landslide on May 1.
Major's Conservatives also championed flexibility but fiercely opposed the employment chapter, saying it would be a blueprint for bureaucratic meddling and would impose extra burdens on companies.
But Cook described it as a modest, sensible step that will require EU institutions to consider the consequences for jobs of any policies before they were adopted.

"The new Labour government has obtained an amendment to the first article of the employment chapter which recognises that, if we are to increase employment, then we must increase employability and increase the flexibility of the labour market," Cook said.
